BLT.summary: Cloud computing fundamentals cover the on-demand, metered provision of computing resources over a network, the service and deployment models, virtualisation and container technologies, and the shared responsibility model. The exam asks about the IaaS/PaaS/SaaS distinction, private/public/hybrid cloud, NIST's five essential characteristics, the difference between a virtual machine and a container, and regulatory expectations for bank cloud use (data residency, outsourcing risk).
concepts: The 5 essential characteristics of the NIST cloud definition: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling (multi-tenant), rapid elasticity, measured service (pay as you go).

Service models: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) virtual machines, storage, network (AWS EC2, Azure VM); PaaS (Platform) runtime and database management with the provider, code with the customer (Heroku, Azure App Service); SaaS (Software) ready-made application (Office 365, Salesforce). FaaS/serverless: event-triggered functions (AWS Lambda).

Deployment models: Public cloud (provider infrastructure, shared), Private cloud (belongs to a single organisation, on-premises or hosted), Hybrid (combination of the two, workloads portable), Community cloud (organisations with common needs, e.g. banks), Multi-cloud (more than one provider).

Shared responsibility model: The provider is responsible for 'security of the cloud' (physical, hypervisor, network infrastructure), the customer for 'security in the cloud' (data, identity, access, configuration, encryption keys). The customer's responsibility is widest in IaaS and narrowest in SaaS.

Virtualisation: A hypervisor runs multiple virtual machines (VMs) on physical hardware. Type 1 (bare-metal: VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen) runs directly on the hardware; Type 2 (hosted: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) runs on top of an operating system. VM escape is breaking into neighbouring VMs through a hypervisor vulnerability.

Container: A lightweight isolation unit that shares the operating system kernel and packages the application with its dependencies (Docker). An image is the template, a container the running instance. Orchestration (Kubernetes) deploys, scales and heals containers in pods.

Scalability: Vertical scaling (scale up, a more powerful machine) and horizontal scaling (scale out, more machines). Auto scaling changes the number of instances according to a load metric; the load balancer distributes traffic. Elasticity is resources automatically growing and shrinking.

Cloud storage types: Object storage (S3, Blob; accessed over HTTP, with metadata, scalable), block storage (EBS; VM disk), file storage (NFS/SMB share). Data tiers hot/cold/archive (Glacier) balance cost against access.

Cloud identity and access management (IAM): Users, groups, roles and policies; the principle of least privilege, the root account not used day to day, MFA, temporary credentials (STS/role assumption). A misconfigured publicly accessible storage bucket is the most common cause of cloud leaks.

Cloud network structures: Virtual private cloud (VPC/VNet), subnets, security groups (stateful instance-level firewall), network ACLs (subnet level), connection to the corporate network via VPN or a private line (Direct Connect/ExpressRoute), redundancy through regions and availability zones.

Cloud security tools: Encryption (KMS/HSM-managed keys for data at rest, TLS in transit), CASB (cloud access security broker), CSPM (configuration auditing), logging (CloudTrail/Activity Log); customer-managed keys (BYOK) increase the organisation's control.

Service level agreement (SLA): Availability percentage (99.9% = ~8.8 hours of downtime per year; 99.99% = ~53 minutes), outage notification periods, data deletion and exit conditions. Vendor lock-in is a portability risk.

Cloud from a bank's perspective: It is a form of outsourcing; risk assessment, the right to audit in the contract, data residency (the expectation that data is kept within the country), exit strategy, business continuity and the BDDK notification/permission processes are evaluated. The location and auditability of primary and secondary systems is a critical issue.

DevOps and cloud: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, CloudFormation) provides repeatable and auditable environments; immutable infrastructure deploys a new image instead of updating a server. Edge computing performs processing close to the data source.

misconceptions: Misconception: When data is moved to the cloud, the provider is entirely responsible for its security. Correct: In the shared responsibility model, data, identity, access rights and configuration are always the customer's responsibility.

Misconception: A container is a lighter version of a virtual machine with the same security. Correct: Containers share the host kernel; a kernel vulnerability affects all containers, so isolation is weaker than a VM.

Misconception: A private cloud is only ever in the organisation's own data centre. Correct: A private cloud is defined by being dedicated to a single organisation; it can be hosted by a third party (hosted private cloud).
Misconception: A 99.9% SLA means almost no downtime. Correct: It permits roughly 8.8 hours of downtime per year; that may be high for critical banking systems.

Misconception: The cloud is always cheaper than an on-premises installation. Correct: For stable and predictable high loads, on-premises can be cheaper in the long run; the cloud has the advantage for variable loads and a fast start.

Misconception: In the cloud, data backup is taken automatically and sufficiently by the provider. Correct: The provider's infrastructure redundancy does not replace a backup strategy that protects the customer from logical errors or deletion; backup is the customer's responsibility.
BLT.example: A bank plans to run its customer communication campaign application as PaaS in the public cloud. In the risk assessment the auditor asks the following questions: In which region will the customer data be kept, and is the data residency expectation met; does the contract give the bank and the regulator the right to audit; are the encryption keys managed by the bank (BYOK); is identity management tied to the corporate directory (SSO + MFA); are the exit strategy and the evidence of data deletion defined. It is verified with a CSPM tool that the storage buckets are not 'public'. The core banking system, because of its sensitivity, stays in the private cloud; this makes it a hybrid model.

SIB.summary: Cybersecurity fundamentals deal with threat, vulnerability and attack types from the attacker's perspective, and with detection, response and security architecture concepts on the defence side. In the exam, the OWASP Top 10 web vulnerabilities (SQL injection, XSS, CSRF), DDoS, man-in-the-middle, the kill chain, SIEM/SOC, penetration test types and incident response steps stand out.
concepts: A threat is a potential event that could cause harm, a vulnerability a weakness that can be exploited, an exploit the code/method that uses the vulnerability, and risk the combination of the likelihood that the threat uses the vulnerability and its impact.

SQL injection: User input being appended directly to the SQL query; authentication is bypassed with payloads such as ' OR '1'='1. Defence: parameterised queries (prepared statements), ORM, a least-privilege database account, input validation.
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): The attacker's script running in the victim's browser. Types: stored, reflected, DOM-based. Defence: output encoding, Content Security Policy, the HttpOnly cookie flag.

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): The logged-in user's browser unknowingly sending a request prepared by the attacker. Defence: anti-CSRF token, SameSite cookie attribute, re-authentication for critical operations.

OWASP Top 10 (2021): A01 Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A04 Insecure Design, A05 Security Misconfiguration, A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components, A07 Identification and Authentication Failures, A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures, A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures, A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).

DoS/DDoS: Making a service unavailable by consuming resources. Volume-based (UDP flood, DNS amplification), protocol-based (SYN flood), application layer (HTTP flood). Defence: rate limiting, SYN cookies, CDN/scrubbing centre.

Man-in-the-Middle (MitM): The attacker inserting themselves between two parties and monitoring or altering the traffic; ARP poisoning, rogue Wi-Fi and SSL stripping are examples. Defence: TLS, certificate pinning, HSTS.
Brute force tries all combinations, a dictionary attack common passwords, credential stuffing leaked password pairs. Defence: account lockout, rate limiting, MFA, strong hashing.

A zero-day is a vulnerability for which there is no patch yet. CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is the vulnerability identifier, CVSS (a score from 0 to 10) the severity metric; 9.0-10.0 counts as critical.

Cyber Kill Chain: Reconnaissance, weaponisation, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control (C2), actions on objectives. MITRE ATT&CK is the matrix that classifies attacker tactics and techniques.

Penetration test types: black box (no information), grey box (partial information), white box (full information). Vulnerability scanning is automated and superficial; a penetration test also attempts exploitation. The red team attacks, the blue team defends.

A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects logs, correlates them and generates alerts; the SOC (Security Operations Center) is the team that monitors them 24/7. EDR performs behaviour-based detection on the endpoint, NDR on the network.

Incident response life cycle (NIST SP 800-61): Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment-Eradication-Recovery, Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned). In digital forensics, a hash is taken for evidence integrity and a chain of custody is maintained.

Zero trust, with the principle 'never trust, always verify', verifies every request according to identity, device and context rather than network location. Network segmentation limits lateral movement.

YIS.summary: Backup and business continuity fundamentals cover the controls that ensure data can be recovered and critical business processes resume within an acceptable time in the face of data loss and service outage risks. The exam asks, through banking scenarios, about backup types (full, incremental, differential), the 3-2-1 rule, the RPO/RTO/MTD concepts, disaster recovery site types (hot/warm/cold), business impact analysis, the difference between a business continuity plan and a disaster recovery plan, and test types.
concepts: Backup is copying data so that it can be recovered in the event of loss, corruption, deletion or ransomware; since the purpose of backup is restore, an untested backup counts for nothing. Archiving is for long-term retention obligations, backup for operational recovery.

Backup types: Full, all data; Incremental, what changed since the last backup (full or incremental), fastest backup, slowest restore (the full + the whole chain of incrementals is needed); Differential, what changed since the last FULL backup, restore is done with the full + the last differential, backup size grows every day. Synthetic full and continuous data protection (CDP) are advanced methods.

Archive bit and restore chain: An incremental backup resets the archive bit, a differential does not. If one incremental backup in the chain is corrupt, the later points cannot be recovered; that is why periodic full backups and integrity verification (hash/checksum) are needed.

3-2-1 rule: At least 3 copies, on 2 different media types, 1 copy at a different location (off-site). The 3-2-1-1-0 extension against ransomware: 1 copy offline or immutable/air-gapped, 0 restore errors (tested). Backups are encrypted and access to them is restricted.

Backup retention and rotation: The retention period is set according to regulatory and business requirements; Grandfather-Father-Son (GFS: daily, weekly, monthly/yearly) rotation is common. Backup media are labelled, inventoried, protected in transit and securely destroyed at end of life.

RPO (Recovery Point Objective): The maximum acceptable period of data loss; it determines the backup/replication frequency (if the RPO is 1 hour, at least hourly backup or asynchronous replication). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): The target time for the service to be running again after an outage. MTD/MTPD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime): The longest outage the business can endure; RTO ≤ MTD must hold. WRT (Work Recovery Time) is the time, after the system is up, to verify the data and return the business to normal: RTO + WRT ≤ MTD.

Business impact analysis (BIA): Identifies the critical business processes, the dependent systems and the financial/reputational/legal impact of an outage growing over time, and assigns MTD, RTO and RPO to each process. The BIA is the foundation of business continuity planning and gives the recovery priority (which system first). The risk assessment determines which threats (earthquake, fire, cyber attack, supplier failure) are to be planned for.

The business continuity plan (BCP) covers sustaining critical business processes (branch service, payment systems) by alternative means during an outage: staff, call tree, alternative workplace, manual procedures, suppliers. The disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the IT-focused subset of the BCP: bringing up the systems and data at the disaster recovery site.

Disaster recovery (DR) site types: Hot (hardware and current data ready, minutes-hours, most expensive), Warm (hardware present, data partly current, hours-days), Cold (only space and infrastructure, days-weeks, cheapest), Mirrored/active-active (synchronous, near-zero RPO/RTO), mobile and reciprocal agreement options. A bank's secondary centre must be in a different risk zone from the primary centre (outside the earthquake fault line).

Data replication: Synchronous, every write is acknowledged once committed on both sides, RPO ≈ 0, there is a distance limit (latency); Asynchronous, delayed copy, RPO seconds-minutes, long distance. Database log shipping, storage-level replication and snapshot techniques are used; a snapshot does not replace a backup because it is on the same storage.

The difference between high availability (HA) and disaster recovery: HA is redundancy at the same location against a single component failure (cluster, RAID, dual power supply, load balancer; no 'single point of failure'); DR is a different location against the loss of the whole site. RAID protects against disk failure but is not a backup against deletion, corruption or ransomware.

Business continuity life cycle (ISO 22301): Policy and scope → BIA and risk assessment → strategy selection → plan development → awareness and training → exercise/test → maintenance and review (annually or after major changes). Copies of the plan are kept off-site and accessible; the call tree and the crisis management team are defined.

Test types (in order of increasing realism): Checklist/read-through, Tabletop/structured walkthrough, Simulation (scenario enactment, production not interrupted), Parallel test (DR systems are brought up, production continues), Full interruption test (production is moved to the DR site, the riskiest and most conclusive). The BDDK expects banks to test their business continuity plans regularly and to demonstrate that the secondary centre can process real transactions.

Restore testing from backup: Periodic restores from randomly selected backups, measurement of duration and data integrity, recording of the results. The auditor asks for the backup logs (failed jobs and retries), compliance with the retention policy, the existence of the off-site copy, encryption and the date of the most recent restore test as evidence.

misconceptions: Misconception: RAID or disk mirroring replaces a backup. Correct: RAID provides availability against disk failure; accidental deletion, data corruption or ransomware affects both copies at the same time. A backup is a separate copy that can be rolled back in time.
Misconception: If backups are being taken, the data is safe. Correct: A backup with no restore test gives no assurance; the auditor asks for evidence of the last successful restore test.

Misconception: Differential backup is another name for incremental backup. Correct: Incremental takes the changes since the last backup of any kind, differential since the last FULL backup; the restore sets and archive bit behaviour differ.

Misconception: RPO and RTO measure the same thing. Correct: RPO measures backward-looking data loss, RTO forward-looking outage duration; zero RPO (synchronous replication) can coexist with an RTO of hours.

Misconception: A cold disaster recovery site is sufficient for banking systems because it is cheap. Correct: A cold site gives an RTO of days-weeks; systems with a low MTD, such as payments and core banking, require a hot or mirrored site.

Misconception: The disaster recovery site can be in the same city as the primary centre, in the same building on a different floor. Correct: It must be in a different risk zone so that it is not affected by the same disaster (earthquake, fire, flood, power outage).
YIS.example: The business impact analysis for the bank's credit card authorisation system has set MTD = 2 hours and RPO = 5 minutes. Currently a full backup is taken at 02:00 at night and an incremental every 6 hours during the day, and the DR site is at warm level. The auditor writes as findings that the 6-hour backup interval does not meet the 5-minute RPO (in the worst case 6 hours of transactions lost) and that the warm site's hours-to-days RTO exceeds the 2-hour MTD. Recommendation: a hot/active-active DR site with synchronous or seconds-delayed asynchronous replication for the database, 3-2-1-1-0 compliance with an immutable copy of the backups, and at least once a year an exercise in which real transactions are processed at the DR site. In addition, if it is seen that the last restore test was carried out 14 months ago, this becomes a second finding.

RISK.summary: The IT risk and controls topic covers identifying, measuring, controlling and monitoring the risks arising from information systems, and how an auditor tests those controls. It is the most critical topic for the bank inspector role: the risk management process, control types (preventive/detective/corrective, general/application controls), the three lines of defence, the COBIT/ISO 27001/BDDK framework, audit evidence and sampling concepts come up in the exam as scenario questions.
concepts: Risk is the combination of the likelihood and the impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability to create an adverse effect on an asset. Inherent risk is the risk with no controls, residual risk is what remains after controls are applied. Risk appetite is the total level of risk the organisation is prepared to accept, tolerance is the acceptable deviation from the target.

Risk management process (ISO 31000 / ISO/IEC 27005 / NIST RMF): Establishing the context → asset inventory and classification → risk identification (threat, vulnerability) → analysis (likelihood, impact) → evaluation (comparison with criteria) → treatment → monitoring and review → communication. The risk register holds all risks, their owners and the treatment plan.

Risk treatment options: Mitigate/control (apply a control), Accept (within appetite, documented and approved by management), Transfer/share (insurance, outsourcing contract; responsibility cannot be fully transferred), Avoid (not carrying out the activity).

Risk analysis methods: Qualitative (low/medium/high matrix, expert judgement, fast), Quantitative (monetary: SLE, ARO, ALE; cost-benefit calculation), Semi-quantitative (scoring). In quantitative analysis, if the cost of the control exceeds the ALE reduction it provides, the control is not economical.

Control: A policy, procedure, practice or technical mechanism designed to reduce risk. By function: Preventive (MFA, segregation of duties, input validation), Detective (audit log review, reconciliation, IDS), Corrective (restore from backup, patch, incident response); also deterrent, compensating and directive (policy, training) controls.

By form of implementation: Administrative (policy, training, hiring controls), Technical/logical (encryption, firewall, access list), Physical (lock, camera, security guard). Automated controls (enforced by the system, consistent) and manual controls (performed by a human, higher margin of error, require sample testing).

IT general controls (ITGC): Controls that affect all applications; access management, change management, IT operations (job scheduling, backup, incident management), program development/acquisition, physical and environmental security. If the ITGCs are weak, application controls cannot be relied upon.

Application controls: Transaction-level controls within a specific business application; input (mandatory field, format, range, check digit, limit check, authority check), processing (control totals, sequence check, duplicate check), output (report distribution control, reconciliation) and interface controls (comparison of sent/received record counts/totals).

Three lines of defence (Three Lines Model): 1st line business units and IT operations (own the risk, operate the controls), 2nd line risk management, compliance and information security (set the framework, monitor), 3rd line internal audit/inspection (provide independent assurance, report to the board/audit committee). External audit and the regulator (BDDK) provide assurance from outside the organisation.

Control testing: Design effectiveness (is the control designed to address the risk; walkthrough) and operating effectiveness (did it work consistently throughout the period; sample testing). Evidence types: inspection (documents), observation, inquiry (weakest on its own), re-performance (strongest), analytical procedures, computer-assisted audit techniques (CAAT: analysing the whole data set, duplicate records, Benford).

Audit risk = Inherent risk × Control risk × Detection risk. If control risk is high, the auditor performs more substantive testing (lowers detection risk). Materiality is the threshold at which a finding influences decision makers. A finding has 5 elements: condition, criteria, cause, effect, recommendation.

IT governance envisaged by the BDDK regulation: Ultimate responsibility of the board of directors, an information systems strategy and risk management process, an information security policy and responsible unit, inclusion of IT processes within the scope of internal control and internal audit, the expectation that primary and secondary systems are kept within the country, risk assessment and the right to audit in outsourcing, reporting of incidents and outages. In addition, periodic information systems audits are carried out by independent audit firms.

COBIT 2019: An IT governance and management framework; 5 domains (EDM Evaluate-Direct-Monitor: governance; APO Align-Plan-Organise; BAI Build-Acquire-Implement; DSS Deliver-Service-Support; MEA Monitor-Evaluate-Assess) and 40 governance/management objectives. APO12 (Managed Risk) stands out for risk, APO13 for security, MEA02 for internal control. Process maturity is measured with capability levels 0-5.

ISO/IEC 27001:2022: Information Security Management System (ISMS) requirements; risk-based approach, scope, leadership, risk assessment and treatment, Statement of Applicability (SoA), Annex A controls (4 themes in 2022: organisational, people, physical, technological; 93 controls), internal audit, management review, continual improvement (PDCA: Plan-Do-Check-Act). ISO 27001 is certifiable, ISO 27002 is the control implementation guide.

misconceptions: Misconception: Accepting a risk is ignoring the risk. Correct: Acceptance is a documented decision by authorised management that the risk has been analysed and remains within appetite; ignoring is a risk that has not been analysed.

Misconception: Transferring a risk to insurance or an outsourcing provider also transfers the responsibility. Correct: The financial impact is shared, but the responsibility towards the regulator and the customer stays with the bank; the BDDK states explicitly that the bank's responsibility continues in outsourcing.
Misconception: Residual risk must be reduced to zero. Correct: There is no zero risk and its cost is infinite; the goal is to bring residual risk down to the appetite/tolerance limit.

Misconception: Inquiry (interviewing management) is sufficient audit evidence on its own. Correct: Inquiry is the weakest type of evidence; it must be supported by document inspection, observation or re-performance.

Misconception: The existence of a control (policy written, tool installed) shows that it is effective. Correct: Design effectiveness is not enough; operating effectiveness must be tested by sampling across the period.

Misconception: Internal audit is the 2nd line of defence. Correct: Internal audit is the 3rd line, providing independent assurance; the 2nd line is the risk management, compliance and information security functions.
RISK.example: The bank's internet banking server suffers an average of 2 service outages per year; the transaction loss and reputational cost of each outage is calculated as 400,000 TL (SLE). ALE = 400,000 × 2 = 800,000 TL. If an investment in a redundant (active-active) architecture and a load balancer, at an annual cost of 300,000 TL, will reduce the outage frequency to 0.25 per year, the new ALE = 100,000 TL; since the reduction achieved is 700,000 TL and the net benefit is 400,000 TL, the control is economically justified. In the report the auditor writes the finding as condition (a single server with no redundancy), criteria (the BDDK's service continuity and risk management expectation, the organisation's 99.9% SLA target), cause (lack of capacity planning), effect (800,000 TL annual expected loss and regulatory reporting risk), recommendation (redundant architecture + monthly KRI monitoring), and asks that management's acceptance of the remaining risk be documented.

GT.summary: The emerging technologies topic covers the fundamental concepts and the risks introduced by the technologies transforming banking, such as artificial intelligence, big data, blockchain, the Internet of Things, 5G, quantum computing, open banking and digital identity. The exam asks definition-level questions (machine learning types, blockchain characteristics, the V's of big data, the API economy) and about the use of these technologies in banking and their audit/compliance consequences.
concepts: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the general name for systems that imitate human intelligence; machine learning (ML) is the subfield that learns patterns from data; deep learning (DL) is the ML subfield using multi-layer artificial neural networks. Generative AI and large language models (LLMs; GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) generate text/code/images.

Machine learning types: Supervised (labelled data; classification e.g. fraud yes/no, regression e.g. credit score), Unsupervised (unlabelled; customer segmentation with clustering, anomaly detection), Reinforcement (trial and error with reward/penalty). Overfitting is memorising the training data without generalising; it is controlled with the training/validation/test split.

AI risks and governance: Data bias and discrimination (in credit decisions), explainability (black-box models), model risk and validation, data privacy, prompt injection and hallucination (LLMs). The EU AI Act (2024) classifies credit scoring as 'high risk'; the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management system) are governance frameworks.

Big data characteristics (the V's): Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value. Technologies: Hadoop (HDFS distributed file system + MapReduce), Apache Spark (in-memory processing), NoSQL databases, the distinction between a data lake (raw data) and a data warehouse (structured, analytical), ETL/ELT processes.

Levels of data analytics: Descriptive (what happened), Diagnostic (why it happened), Predictive (what will happen), Prescriptive (what to do). Data governance defines data ownership, quality, dictionary and lineage; KVKK (Turkish Personal Data Protection Law, Law No. 6698) and GDPR regulate the conditions for processing personal data; anonymisation and pseudonymisation protect privacy in analytics.

Blockchain: A distributed and immutable ledger of time-stamped blocks linked by cryptographic hashes; consensus mechanisms Proof of Work (Bitcoin, energy intensive), Proof of Stake (Ethereum after 2022). Public/permissionless and permissioned/consortium (Hyperledger Fabric, R3 Corda) networks; banks prefer permissioned networks.

A smart contract is code on the blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met; code errors can cause irreversible damage (the DAO attack). Crypto-assets, stablecoins, central bank digital currency (CBDC; the Digital Turkish Lira project is run by the TCMB) and tokenisation (digital representation of assets) are applications relevant to banking. Blockchain does not solve every problem; a central database is faster and cheaper in most cases.

Internet of Things (IoT): Sensors and embedded devices connected to the internet; ATM/POS telemetry, smart branches, wearable payments. Risks: weak default passwords, missing patches, botnets (Mirai), a wide attack surface; network segmentation and device identity management are the defences. Edge computing processes data close to the source.

5G: High bandwidth, very low latency (~1 ms target), dense device support, network slicing. Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control and data planes; network function virtualisation (NFV) moves hardware appliances into software; SD-WAN manages branch connections centrally.

Quantum computing: The qubit, through superposition and entanglement, speeds up certain problems exponentially. Shor's algorithm threatens RSA and ECC, Grover's algorithm symmetric key search (it halves the effective key length: AES-128 → 64 bits effective, which is why AES-256 is recommended). The transition to post-quantum cryptography (NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA; 2024) is planned from today against the 'harvest now, decrypt later' risk; crypto agility is the ability to swap algorithms.

Open banking and the API economy: The bank opening account information (AISP) and payment initiation (PISP) services to third parties through standard APIs with the customer's consent; PSD2 in Europe, in Türkiye the TCMB's payment services and data sharing services regulations and BKM's open banking API infrastructure (phased in from 2021-2022). Risks: API security (OAuth 2.0, strong customer authentication), third-party risk, data sharing consent. BaaS (Banking as a Service) and fintech partnerships rest on this infrastructure.

Digital identity and payment innovations: Remote customer onboarding (identity verification by video; BDDK 2021 regulation), e-Government and e-signature/mobile signature, biometric authentication, FAST (the TCMB's instant payment system, 24/7), QR code payments, contactless and tokenised card payments (similar to Apple Pay/Google Pay), digital wallets. In fraud, deepfakes and synthetic identities are new threats.

Regulatory technology (RegTech) and supervisory technology (SupTech): AI and data analytics in compliance monitoring, suspicious transaction reporting (MASAK, the Turkish financial crimes investigation board), know-your-customer (KYC/AML) processes; continuous auditing and continuous monitoring let the auditor work on the whole data set instead of a sample.

Current approaches in cybersecurity: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207), SASE (network + security converged in the cloud), XDR (extended detection and response), security automation (SOAR), AI-assisted threat detection and attackers also using AI (automated phishing, deepfake voice fraud). Ransomware as a Service (RaaS) and supply chain attacks (SolarWinds 2020) are prominent threats.

Grover effect: the quantum effective security of an n-bit symmetric key ≈ n/2 bits (AES-128 → 64 bits, AES-256 → 128 bits)
Classification metrics: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/Total; Precision = TP/(TP+FP); Recall = TP/(TP+FN); F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R)
In fraud detection, a false positive = blocking a legitimate transaction (customer dissatisfaction), a false negative = missing the fraud (financial loss)
misconceptions: Misconception: Blockchain data is confidential because it is encrypted. Correct: On a public blockchain, transactions can be read by anyone; cryptography is used for immutability and signatures, not for confidentiality. Confidentiality requires a permissioned network or additional techniques.

Misconception: If an AI model gives high accuracy, it is fair and reliable. Correct: On imbalanced data, 99% accuracy can be meaningless (calling every transaction 'clean'); moreover, historical data bias leads to discriminatory decisions. Precision/recall and fairness metrics are assessed together.

Misconception: Quantum computers break all encryption. Correct: Shor's algorithm breaks asymmetric ciphers such as RSA/ECC; symmetric ciphers such as AES are only weakened by Grover, and increasing the key size is sufficient.

Misconception: The data lake replaces the data warehouse. Correct: The two meet different needs; the lake is raw and flexible, the warehouse structured and optimised for reporting. Modern architectures combine the two (lakehouse).

Misconception: Open banking is the bank sharing customer data without permission. Correct: Sharing happens only with the customer's explicit consent, to authorised third parties, with strong authentication and standard APIs.

Misconception: The information given by generative AI is always correct. Correct: LLMs can produce hallucinations (fabrications) and are open to prompt injection; in banking, human review and source verification of the outputs are required.
GT.example: The bank is deploying a supervised machine learning model to detect fraud in card transactions in real time. The model is trained with historical labelled transactions (fraud/clean); since only 0.1% of transactions are fraud, the accuracy metric is misleading, so the team monitors precision and recall. Within the scope of model risk, the auditor asks: was bias against particular customer groups tested in the training data, are the decisions explainable (a justification in case of a customer objection), is model performance degrading over time (drift) and does retraining go through change management, is the personal data used by the model processed in compliance with KVKK. In addition, card tokenisation and the irrevocability of instant payments via FAST make it mandatory for detection to happen within milliseconds; that is why the model is run in a low-latency architecture close to the endpoint.
